knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")

```{r setup}
library(bssd)
```

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
# results and settings of the installed reproduction and validation scripts
read_results <- function(folder, name) {
  read.csv(system.file(folder, "results", name, package = "bssd",
                       mustWork = TRUE), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
# value assigned at the top level of an installed validation script
script_value <- function(script, name) {
  exprs <- parse(system.file("validation", script, package = "bssd",
                             mustWork = TRUE))
  for (e in exprs) {
    if (is.call(e) && identical(e[[1L]], as.name("<-")) &&
        identical(e[[2L]], as.name(name))) {
      return(eval(e[[3L]], baseenv()))
    }
  }
  stop("'", name, "' is not assigned in ", script, call. = FALSE)
}
fmt <- function(x, digits = 4) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
fmt_e <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1)
fmt_n <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
# MCMC comparisons of a validation script. The tolerance of each item is four
# Monte Carlo standard errors. For the median, the reference is 0.5 and the
# compared value is the MCMC proportion of draws below the bssd median.
mcmc_table <- function(v, rr = "r") {
  v <- v[v$judgement != "INFO", ]
  stat <- sub("^.*_", "", v$id)
  med <- stat == "MED"
  quantity <- stat
  is_p <- grepl("^P[0-9]", stat)
  quantity[is_p] <- sprintf("P(%s > %s)", rr, sub("^P", "", stat[is_p]))
  quantity[stat == "PROB"] <- sub(" [|] data[)].*$", ")",
                                  v$quantity[stat == "PROB"])
  quantity[med] <- sprintf("P(%s <= bssd median)", rr)
  quantity[stat == "MEAN"] <- sprintf("mean of %s", rr)
  quantity[stat == "IPP"] <- "placebo incidence"
  quantity[stat == "IPD"] <- "study drug incidence"
  bssd_value <- ifelse(med, v$reference, v$bssd)
  mcmc_value <- ifelse(med, v$bssd, v$reference)
  data.frame(data = sub("^[A-Z]+_([A-Z][0-9]+)_.*$", "\\1", v$id),
             quantity = quantity, bssd = bssd_value, mcmc = mcmc_value,
             difference = bssd_value - mcmc_value, se = v$tolerance / 4,
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
show_mcmc <- function(m) {
  knitr::kable(data.frame(Data = m$data, Quantity = m$quantity,
                          bssd = fmt(m$bssd), MCMC = fmt(m$mcmc),
                          Difference = fmt_e(m$difference),
                          SE = fmt_e(m$se),
                          Ratio = fmt(abs(m$difference) / m$se, 2)),
               align = "llrrrrr")
}
# effective sample sizes of the posterior probabilities P(r > c)
ess_range <- function(v) {
  note <- v$note[grepl("_(PROB|P[0-9.]+)$", v$id)]
  range(as.numeric(sub("^.*ESS ([0-9]+).*$", "\\1", note)))
}
# comparison of the default integration grid with a finer grid or with the
# Python reference (validate_convergence.R)
show_convergence <- function(v) {
  parts <- regmatches(v$quantity, regexec(paste0(
    "^(.*), (finer grid vs default|Python reference vs default|",
    "Python reference vs finer grid), (.*)$"), v$quantity))
  parts <- do.call(rbind, parts)
  err <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sub("^reported error ", "", v$note)))
  knitr::kable(data.frame(Data = parts[, 4], Comparison = parts[, 3],
                          Quantity = sub(" [|] data[)]$", ")", parts[, 2]),
                          Reference = fmt(v$reference, 6),
                          bssd = fmt(v$bssd, 6),
                          Difference = fmt_e(v$abs_diff),
                          `Error estimate` = ifelse(is.na(err), "",
                                                    fmt_e(err)),
                          check.names = FALSE),
               align = "lllrrrr")
}
```

## Model

BDRIBS(2) is the modification of BDRIBS(1) examined by Duncan (2026,
Section 3.2.3): the total exposure time is replaced by the total time at
risk, in which the time after the first occurrence of the event is
discarded. For subject $i$ with the follow-up time $t_i$ and the time to the
first event $s_i$ ($s_i = \infty$ for a subject without the event), the two
exposures are
$$E_1 = \sum_i t_i \quad \text{(BDRIBS(1))}, \qquad E_2 = \sum_i \min(t_i, s_i) \quad \text{(BDRIBS(2))}.$$
The rest of the model is that of BDRIBS(1) (`vignette("bdribs1")`):
$$Y \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\{E_2 \delta (r k + 1) / (k + 1)\}, \quad \delta \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\lambda_{HP} PT_{HP} / DF, PT_{HP} / DF), \quad r = \frac{p}{k (1 - p)}, \quad p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b).$$

The number of subjects with the event, $Y$, counts first events only, and a
subject cannot have a first event after it. With the total exposure time,
this time is still counted as exposure, so that the exposure is too large
for the observed number of events. Duncan (2026, Section 3.2.3) notes that
the distinction has no impact for small incidences and a noticeable impact
for larger ones, and BDRIBS(1) has lower power than BDRIBS(2) at medium and
high incidences (Duncan, 2026, Section 4.1).

BDRIBS(2) uses the same function as BDRIBS(1), `bdribs_post()`, with the
total time at risk as `exposure`. The other arguments are described in
`vignette("bdribs1")`. `time_at_risk()` computes both exposures from
subject-level data.

## Example

The following data are simulated with `sim_blinded()` with incidences of the
high-incidence scenarios of Duncan (2026, Table 1): 200 subjects randomized
1:1 with uniform entry over 26 weeks, 52 weeks of follow-up, and exponential
times to the event with cumulative incidences of 30% on placebo and 45% on
the study drug at week 52. The blinded analysis is at week 78, when all
subjects have completed follow-up.

```{r data}
set.seed(2026)
rate_of <- function(ip, t) -log(1 - ip) / t
d <- sim_blinded(n = 200, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 52,
                 analysis_time = 78, dist = "exponential",
                 par_p = rate_of(0.30, 52), par_d = rate_of(0.45, 52))
tar <- time_at_risk(d$follow_up, d$event, d$event_time)
tar
```

The total time at risk is
`r round(100 * tar[["time_at_risk"]] / tar[["exposure"]])`% of the total
exposure time. The prior of $\delta$ is based on a historical placebo group
of 100 subjects followed for 52 weeks with the incidence of 30%, discounted
by $DF = 2$.

```{r fit}
fits <- list(
  BDRIBS1 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]], exposure = tar[["exposure"]],
                        k = 1, lambda_hp = rate_of(0.30, 52),
                        pt_hp = 100 * 52, df = 2, t_star = 52),
  BDRIBS2 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]],
                        exposure = tar[["time_at_risk"]], k = 1,
                        lambda_hp = rate_of(0.30, 52), pt_hp = 100 * 52,
                        df = 2, t_star = 52)
)
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, summary))
res$model <- names(fits)
knitr::kable(res[, c("model", "prob", "signal", "rr_median", "ip_placebo",
                     "ip_drug", "ip_difference")], digits = 3,
             row.names = FALSE)
```

The last three columns are the posterior means of the cumulative incidences
at week 52 and of their difference; the true values are 0.30, 0.45 and 0.15.
The posterior means of the placebo incidence are
`r fmt(res$ip_placebo[1], 3)` with the total exposure time and
`r fmt(res$ip_placebo[2], 3)` with the total time at risk.

## Operating characteristics

```{r oc-data, include = FALSE}
sim <- read_results("reproduce", "reproduce_Duncan2026_simulation.csv")
design <- read_results("reproduce", "Duncan2026_simulation_design.csv")
des <- design[design$figure %in% c(3, 4), ]
power_of <- function(model) {
  ids <- sprintf("D_SIM_%s_P%d_L1_%s_power", des$figure, des$point, model)
  sim$reproduced[match(ids, sim$id)]
}
threshold <- sub("^.*threshold ([0-9.]+)[)].*$", "\\1",
                 sim$quantity[match(sprintf("D_SIM_%s_P%d_L1_BDRIBS1_power",
                                            des$figure, des$point), sim$id)])
oc <- data.frame(
  Figure = des$figure,
  Placebo = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - exp(-as.numeric(des$par_p) *
                                                des$follow_up))),
  `Study drug` = sub("^drug ", "", des$label), N = des$n,
  `Analysis (week)` = round(as.numeric(des$analysis_time), 1),
  Threshold = threshold,
  `BDRIBS(1)` = power_of("BDRIBS1"), `BDRIBS(2)` = power_of("BDRIBS2"),
  check.names = FALSE)
judgement_of <- function(id) sim$judgement[match(id, sim$id)]
```

The folder `reproduce` of the installed package contains the simulations of
Figures 2 to 10 of Duncan (2026) with `r fmt_n(unique(des$n_sim))` simulated
trials per scenario. For the medium (Figure 3) and high (Figure 4) incidences,
the proportions of trials with a signal (power) of the two models are

```{r oc-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(oc, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The incidences are at week 52. BDRIBS(1) has much lower power than BDRIBS(2),
as stated by Duncan (2026, Section 4.1); the corresponding statements of the
article are judged `r judgement_of("D_Q_F3a")` (Figure 3) and
`r judgement_of("D_Q_F4a")` (Figure 4) in
`inst/reproduce/reproduce_Duncan2026_figures.R`. The article does not report
all settings of the simulations, so the published powers are not reproduced
exactly; `results/SUMMARY.md` in the folder `reproduce` gives the details.

## Numerical integration and comparison with MCMC

The posterior computation of BDRIBS(2) is that of BDRIBS(1) with another
exposure. The numerical integration is described in `vignette("bdribs1")`,
and the comparison with MCMC is repeated here.

```{r mcmc-data, include = FALSE}
v <- read_results("validation", "validate_bdribs_package.csv")
m <- mcmc_table(v)
cases <- script_value("validate_bdribs_package.R", "cases")
n_iter <- script_value("validate_bdribs_package.R", "n_iter")
n_chain <- script_value("validate_bdribs_package.R", "n_chain")
src <- readLines(system.file("validation", "validate_bdribs_package.R",
                             package = "bssd", mustWork = TRUE))
n_burn <- as.numeric(sub("^.*burn = ([0-9]+).*$", "\\1",
                         grep("burn = [0-9]+", src, value = TRUE)[1L]))
ess <- ess_range(v)
is_prob <- grepl("^P[(]", m$quantity)
```

The bdribs package of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018) samples the same model by
MCMC with JAGS. The script `inst/validation/validate_bdribs_package.R`
compares `bdribs_post()` with `bdribs::bdribs()` for the settings below, in
which E is the exposure given to both functions. The results in this section
are read from the output of that script (`validate_bdribs_package.csv` in the
folder `validation/results` of the installed package); JAGS is not run when
this article is built.

```{r mcmc-settings, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Data = cases$id, y = cases$y, E = cases$pyr, k = cases$k,
  `Historical events` = cases$bg_events,
  `Historical patient-years` = cases$bg_pyr,
  `Background rate` = ifelse(cases$inf_type == 1, "fixed (inf.type = 1)",
                             "Gamma prior (inf.type = 2)"),
  `Prior of p` = sprintf("Beta(%g, %g)", cases$a, cases$b),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
```

`bdribs::bdribs()` was run with `r n_chain` chains, `r fmt_n(n_burn)`
burn-in iterations and `r fmt_n(n_iter)` iterations. The Monte Carlo
standard error (SE) of each MCMC estimate uses the effective sample size of
the draws
(`coda::effectiveSize()`); for the posterior probabilities, the effective
sample sizes are between `r fmt_n(ess[1])` and `r fmt_n(ess[2])`. For the
median, the table shows the MCMC proportion of draws below the posterior
median computed by bssd, which should be 0.5. The column Ratio is the
absolute difference divided by the SE.

```{r mcmc-table, echo = FALSE}
show_mcmc(m)
```

In all `r nrow(m)` items, the bssd value is within
`r fmt(max(abs(m$difference) / m$se), 1)` standard errors of the MCMC value,
and `r sum(abs(m$difference) / m$se <= 2)` items are within two standard
errors. The largest absolute difference in a posterior probability is
`r fmt(max(abs(m$difference[is_prob])))`, while the SEs of the MCMC
probabilities are between `r fmt(min(m$se[is_prob]))` and
`r fmt(max(m$se[is_prob]))`. Differences of this size are expected from the
Monte Carlo error of MCMC alone, so the difference between the numerical
integration of bssd and MCMC is negligible in practice. The validation script
judges an item PASS when the difference is at most four standard errors;
`r sum(v$judgement == "PASS")` of the `r nrow(v)` items are PASS.

## References

Duncan, B. (2026). Robust safety monitoring and signal detection using
alternatives to the standard Poisson distribution. *Journal of
Biopharmaceutical Statistics*, 36(2), 227-244.
<https://doi.org/10.1080/10543406.2024.2395532>

Mukhopadhyay, S., Waterhouse, B., and Hartford, A. (2018). Bayesian
detection of potential risk using inference on blinded safety data.
*Pharmaceutical Statistics*, 17(6), 823-834.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.1898>
